newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Defector said to repent "sins" - Manila officials.
newsitem.headline: Defector said to repent "sins" - Manila officials.

text.p: North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop told Philippine officials he regretted the mistakes he made while serving the Pyongyang regime and planned to spend the rest of life rectifying them, official sources said on Sunday.

A high-ranking official said arrangements for Hwang's journey to Seoul on Sunday, capping a nine-week cloak-and-dagger diplomatic drama, were finalised after North Korea agreed not to make trouble in exchange for food aid.
"They (the North Koreans) ultimately agreed to his going to the South but in exchange for food aid. That was the clincher," said the official, requesting anonymity.
Sheltered by the Philippines for 33 days, Pyongyang's top ideologue spent most of his time reading and writing in an undisclosed army camp, asking to be left alone, the sources said.

A senior official, asking not to be named, said Hwang expressed regrets at the "sins" he committed as a member of North Korea's government and that Hwang said he planned "to spend the rest of his life" making up for them.
Manila had kept Hwang's Philippine hideout a tightly guarded secret fearing he might be a target of Pyongyang hitmen.
President Fidel Ramos announced Hwang's departure by a special Air Philippines 737 plane only after it had left Philippine airspace.
The officials said South Korea offered to handle Hwang's transportation to Seoul but Manila declined.
They said the Philippines feared flights out of Seoul were being closely watched and any plane leaving South Korea to fetch Hwang might be detected.

"Anything can happen during the three-hour flight," one official said. "It would be easy to take off from Pyongyang. They are still in a Cold War. To the North Koreans, the life of that man no longer has any value."
Despite Hwang's departure, Philippine intelligence officials who handled his security still refused to divulge his hideout, saying they might have use for it again in future.
"It will only reveal our modus operandi," armed forces intelligence chief Major General Benjamin Libarnes told Reuters.
The Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper said Hwang was kept mainly at the sprawling Fort Magsaysay army camp 100 km (60 miles) north of Manila.
"He spent most of the time writing papers, I think, his memoirs," Libarnes said.
"His principal request was to be left alone because he wanted to reflect on the things he must do," said Alfredo Filler, head of the civilian National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICA).
A double-layer security comprising South Koreans and Filipinos kept watch over Hwang 24 hours a day. They were only a few but were "specially trained to protect VIPS", Filler said.
Officials said the Philippines wanted to keep Hwang only for two weeks but allowed him to stay longer on China's request.
"China felt the longer he stayed here the better because it would erase their role in the affair," one official said.
Beijing found itself caught in the Cold War confrontation between its long-time communist ally and new-found capitalist friend when Hwang defected in Beijing on February 12.
Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon denied Hwang was debriefed by South Korean officials during his Philippine stay.
"There was no debriefing. That was our condition," Siazon said.
